title: Trig Equations with Factoring and Multiple Angles
short: Factor, use identities, and handle 2θ and 3θ.
trouble: Students divide both sides by sin x and lose the solutions where sin x = 0.

blocks.html: Harder trig equations come down to the basic ones, using three tools you already have: factoring, identities such as the double-angle formulas, and a careful count of how many turns a multiple angle makes.

(1) If it is quadratic in $\sin x$ or $\cos x$, factor it like $au^2 + bu + c$. (2) If a trig function is a common factor, move everything to one side and factor it out; never divide it away. (3) Use identities to get one function of one angle. (4) For $\sin(kx) = c$ on $[0, 2\pi)$, solve for $kx$ on $[0, 2k\pi)$, then divide by $k$.

Factoring works because of the zero product property: $AB = 0$ exactly when $A = 0$ or $B = 0$. Dividing both sides by $\sin x$ silently assumes $\sin x \ne 0$, so every solution with $\sin x = 0$ disappears. For multiple angles, as $x$ runs once around, $kx$ runs around $k$ times, picking up $k$ times as many solutions.

blocks.name: graph
blocks.cap: $2\sin x\cos x = \sin x$: the curves meet at four places in $[0, 2\pi)$, including the two where $\sin x = 0$.

blocks.title: A common factor
steps: Move everything to one side: $2\sin x\cos x - \sin x = 0$.

blocks.title: A double angle
steps: Let $u = 2x$. As $x$ runs over $[0, 2\pi)$, $u$ runs over $[0, 4\pi)$: two turns.
$\sin u = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ at $u = \frac{\pi}{3}, \frac{2\pi}{3}$ in the first turn, and $\frac{7\pi}{3}, \frac{8\pi}{3}$ in the second.

blocks.title: Use an identity
steps: Use $\cos 2x = 2\cos^2 x - 1$ so only $\cos x$ remains: $2\cos^2 x - \cos x - 1 = 0$.

blocks.html: Dividing both sides of $2\sin x\cos x = \sin x$ by $\sin x$. You get $\cos x = \frac{1}{2}$ and lose $x = 0$ and $x = \pi$. Factor instead. Check your list against a graph: count the crossings.
